key_insight: The paper shows that robotic policies often fail to generalize compositionally because they rely on biased shortcuts tied to specific instruction factors like color, verb, object, size, and spatial cues. It proposes a bias-aware evaluation and data collection strategy to identify and reduce these failures, helping models learn more robust language grounding.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of compositional generalization in robotic manipulation, where pretrained and fine-tuned policies may follow easy visual cues instead of correctly interpreting full instructions. This leads to poor performance on novel instruction combinations.
method: Introduces a diagnostic framework that localizes errors to individual instruction factors such as color, verb, object, size, and spatial attribute.
Formalizes instruction factor bias to measure when policies over-rely on shortcut cues during fine-tuning and evaluation.
Uses bias-aware evaluation and targeted data collection to improve coverage of weak instruction factors and support more compositional learning.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical way to detect why robotic policies fail and where training data is insufficient. It can improve benchmark design, data collection strategy, and the reliability of language-conditioned robot manipulation systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing instruction factors flowing into a robot policy and highlighting shortcut vs grounded behavior
Heatmap or matrix of factor-level bias across color, verb, object, size, and spatial attributes
Before/after comparison chart of standard evaluation versus bias-aware evaluation
Icon set for language, perception, action, and data collection to summarize the framework
paper_title: Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation and Data Collection for Robotic Manipulation
paper_authors: Yu Qi, Zhang Ye, Xinyi Xu, Yuxuan Lu, Amitoj Sandhu
